quickAnswer: Milford's housing is older, denser and more rental than most of MetroWest: 68.9% of homes were built before 1980, 31.7% sit in multi-unit buildings, and 35.6% still heat with oil. Mass HVAC is based in Milford.
body: ## Older, denser and more rental than the middle MetroWest town

Mass HVAC is based in Milford, and the Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) shows why the work here looks different from a typical suburb. Of 11,950 housing units, 2,842 (23.8%) date from 1939 or earlier, the 6th-highest share among the 50 towns we serve, and 68.9% were built before 1980, against 57.2% for the middle town. The median Milford home was built in 1970. Only 491 homes, 4.1%, have gone up since 2010.

Milford was first settled in 1662 and incorporated on April 11, 1780. Pink granite from its quarries built landmarks such as Memorial Hall and drove the local economy until about 1940, and Milford Hospital, donated in 1903 by Governor Eben Sumner Draper, is now Milford Regional Medical Center. Buildings from several eras stand side by side, so heating and cooling needs change a lot from one block to the next.
## How Milford homes are heated

Utility gas heats 5,339 occupied homes (46.6%), but fuel oil is close behind at 4,079 homes (35.6%), near the 36.5% of the middle town. Electricity heats 1,487 homes (13.0%) and bottled or tank gas another 423 (3.7%). That mix matters when a boiler or furnace fails. An oil system needs a yearly cleaning, a gas system depends on a main reaching your street, and an electric or propane home is a natural candidate for a heat pump. We check which of these applies to your address before recommending a replacement.
## Duplexes, small apartment buildings and rental heat

Almost a third of Milford homes (3,791, 31.7%) are in multi-unit buildings, about twice the 16.1% of the middle town. 1,286 units are in two-family buildings (10.8%), 938 in buildings of three or four units (7.8%) and 1,567 in buildings of five or more (13.1%). Renters live in 3,381 households, 29.5% of the town and the 8th-highest share of the 50 towns.

The Town's 2024 Comprehensive Plan notes that nearly 60% of Milford's rental housing was built in the 1950s or earlier, most of it before 1940, and that older rentals are more likely to have deferred maintenance and inefficient heating and cooling systems. For a landlord, a dead boiler in a two-family house leaves two households cold at once. During the heating season, Massachusetts requires rental units to stay at least 68 F from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. and 64 F overnight (105 CMR 410.201). Our Milford [steam boiler replacement in a duplex](/projects/boiler-replacement-milford), with a Weil-McLain boiler, took 48 hours.
## Three neighborhoods the town's own plan names

- **Downtown:** the area around Town Hall and the Milford Town Library, with specialty shops that cater to Milford's Brazilian community.
- **The Plains:** the area between Sacred Heart Church and the junctions of Routes 16 and 109.
- **Prospect Heights:** a section built by the Draper Corporation of Hopedale, which the plan describes as the world's largest manufacturer of automatic looms, between upper Water Street, Route 140 and Milford Hospital.
We work across all three and along Routes 16, 85, 109 and 140 and Interstate 495.
## The utility behind the rebates

Milford's electric utility is National Grid, a Mass Save sponsor, according to the town's own community electricity page, so Mass Save incentives are open to many Milford customers. The amounts and the conditions are on the [heat pump page](/cities/milford/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: Do I need a permit to replace a furnace or boiler in Milford, MA?
faq.a: Usually yes. In Milford, gas permits are issued by the town's Building & Inspections department at 66 Dilla St, and only licensed plumbers may apply for plumbing or gas permits. State rules exempt simple jobs such as replacing the controls on an existing gas appliance, but installing a new gas furnace or boiler normally needs a permit and a final inspection. Ask any contractor who will pull the permit, and call (508) 634-2313 if you are unsure.

faq.q: Who pays for heat in a Milford rental?
faq.a: Unless the lease says otherwise, the landlord pays for heat under the State Sanitary Code. If the heat is out, tell the landlord in writing and keep a copy. This is general information, not legal advice. If you own a Milford duplex or small rental building and the heat fails, call us 24/7 at (508) 786-8755.

faq.q: Most Milford homes are older. Does that change which system I should choose?
faq.a: It can. With 68.9% of homes built before 1980, insulation, air sealing and ductwork vary widely from house to house. Sizing the system to your actual house matters more than the brand, because an oversized system wastes money and an undersized one cannot keep up in January. That is why we assess your home's heating load before we quote.

faq.q: Is natural gas available on my street in Milford?
faq.a: Gas heats 46.6% of occupied Milford homes and oil heats 35.6%, so both are common. Whether a gas main runs past your house depends on the street. Ask the gas company, or ask us during the estimate, because the answer decides whether a conversion, a new oil system or a heat pump makes the most sense.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: About 4,079 Milford homes heat with oil and 5,339 with gas, in houses with a median build year of 1970. We size a new furnace or boiler from your house, not from the unit you are replacing.
body: ## Replacing heat in a town split between oil and gas

A failed furnace or boiler forces a decision, and in Milford the right answer depends on what is already in the basement. Oil heats 35.6% of occupied homes here and utility gas 46.6%, so a like-for-like swap, a conversion to gas where a main is available, and a move to heat pumps all come up in a normal week. The houses are mostly older too: the median home dates to 1970, and 2,842 homes were built in 1939 or earlier.
### What we look at first

- The fuel you have now and what is available on your street.
- How well the house holds heat. Older construction often leaks air, which changes the size of the equipment you need.
- Where the pipes or ducts run, since a boiler swap in a plaster-and-radiator house is a different job from a furnace swap.
- Venting and the gas piping, which decide what the permit inspection will look for.
### Boilers in multi-family buildings

With 31.7% of Milford homes in multi-unit buildings, many repairs involve one boiler serving more than one household. Steam and hot-water systems in older multi-family buildings need careful piping and a pressure test, and the job should be planned around the days the building can be without heat. Our [steam boiler replacement in a Milford duplex](/projects/boiler-replacement-milford) took 48 hours.
### Emergency calls
If the heat goes out, call (508) 786-8755. We take emergency calls 24 hours a day, and we give you a written estimate before work starts.

faq.q: Should I switch from oil to gas when I replace my Milford boiler?
faq.a: It depends on whether a gas main reaches your street and what it costs to connect. A conversion is not always the best choice: some households do better with a new oil boiler, and others with a heat pump. We compare the options for your address at the estimate.

faq.q: How long does a boiler replacement take?
faq.a: It depends on the system. Our steam boiler replacement in a Milford duplex took 48 hours. A simpler furnace swap is usually quicker, and we will give you a schedule with the written estimate.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Milford is 57.1% detached houses, 11.1% attached homes and 31.7% multi-unit buildings, and each cools differently. We match the system to the building, whether that means ducts or none.
body: ## Cooling three kinds of Milford home

According to the 2022 ACS, 6,823 Milford homes are single-family detached houses (57.1%), 1,324 are attached homes such as townhouses (11.1%), and the rest sit in buildings of two or more units. A detached house can often take a central system if the ducts are right. An attached home shares walls and has less room for equipment. An apartment in a small building may have no duct space at all.
### When the house has no ducts

Many older homes were built before central air was common, and Milford's median home dates to 1970. In houses heated by radiators there are usually no ducts to reuse, which is where ductless mini-splits earn their keep: one outdoor unit and a small indoor head for each area you want to cool, with no walls opened up for ductwork.
### Where we start

- Which rooms actually get hot, and why: a top-floor bedroom, a sunny kitchen or a finished attic.
- Where an outdoor unit can sit, which matters most on tight city lots and in attached homes.
- Whether the electrical panel has room for new equipment.
- Whether a heat pump, which cools in summer and heats in winter, would serve you better than cooling alone.
### Apartments and two-family houses

1,286 Milford units are in two-family buildings and 938 in buildings of three or four units. Where tenants pay their own electric bill, a separate ductless system for each apartment lets every household control and pay for its own cooling, and one failed unit does not leave the other apartments without cooling.
### Sizing and humidity

Bigger is not better. An oversized air conditioner cools the air quickly, then shuts off before it has pulled the moisture out, and the house feels clammy. Sizing the equipment from the house itself, including its insulation, windows and orientation, gives steadier temperatures and fewer breakdowns.
Electricity already heats 1,487 Milford homes (13.0%), and for those households a heat pump can cover both seasons from one system.

faq.q: Can I cool a Milford house that has radiators and no ducts?
faq.a: Yes. A ductless mini-split cools without any ductwork, and a technician can install one indoor head per area. Whether a few heads or a full system makes sense depends on the layout of the house.

faq.q: Is there room for central air in a two-family house?
faq.a: Sometimes, but it depends on duct space and on whether the units are separate. Many two-family buildings do better with a ductless system for each apartment, so each household controls its own cooling.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: Mass Save's 2026 whole-home heat pump rebate is $2,650 per ton up to $8,500 per home, and Milford's electric utility, National Grid, is a Mass Save sponsor. The catch is the weatherization condition, and Milford has older homes.
body: ## Heat pump rebates for Milford homes

National Grid is Milford's electric utility and a Mass Save sponsor, so the standard Mass Save heat pump rebates apply to its customers. For equipment installed from January 1 to December 31, 2026, the whole-home air source heat pump rebate is $2,650 per ton, up to $8,500 per home, with one whole-home rebate per customer account. Applications are due by February 28, 2027, the work has to be done by an eligible Mass Save heat pump installer, and income-qualified households may receive more. Program terms can change, so confirm them at masssave.com.
### The weatherization condition

A whole-home rebate requires the home to be sufficiently weatherized first. That is met if the home was built in 2000 or later, if a Mass Save Home Energy Assessment recommends less than $1,000 of weatherization work, or if recommendations made in 2013 or later were completed. In Milford only 10.6% of homes date from 2000 or later, while 68.9% predate 1980, so a large share of owners will start with an assessment and some air sealing or insulation.
### Who gains the most

Homes heated with oil (4,079 in Milford) or bottled gas (423) are the usual candidates, because a heat pump replaces a fuel they buy by delivery. Homes with baseboard electric heat can also benefit. Partial-home rebates exist for houses that keep a fossil-fuel system for the coldest days.
### Mini-splits for apartments and additions

With 31.7% of Milford homes in multi-unit buildings, a ductless mini-split can heat and cool one apartment, a finished attic or a sunroom without touching the rest of the building. See the [cooling page](/cities/milford/air-conditioning-installation-repair) for how ductless fits the town's mix of homes.

faq.q: Does my Milford home qualify for the whole-home heat pump rebate?
faq.a: It qualifies if you are a National Grid customer, the equipment is installed in 2026 by an eligible installer, and the home is sufficiently weatherized. If it was built before 2000, a Home Energy Assessment is the usual route. Rebate terms can change, so check masssave.com.

faq.q: Can I keep my boiler and add a heat pump?
faq.a: Yes. A partial-home setup keeps the existing system for the coldest days while the heat pump carries most of the year. The Mass Save partial-home rebate is $1,125 per ton, up to $8,500, with extra bonuses for weatherization and sizing.

faq.q: Do heat pumps work in Massachusetts winters?
faq.a: Cold-climate heat pumps are designed for them and are the type Mass Save rebates target. Sizing and the quality of the installation matter more than the brand, which is why we calculate the heating load of your house before we quote.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: Oil heats 35.6% of Milford homes, and oil systems need a yearly cleaning. With 29.5% of households renting, many tune-ups are for owners who keep a building running for tenants.
body: ## Tune-ups that fit how Milford heats and rents

Maintenance is not one job. For the 4,079 Milford homes that burn oil, it means cleaning the burner and boiler or furnace every year, changing the filter and nozzle and checking the combustion. For the 5,339 homes on gas, it means a safety and efficiency check of the burner, venting and controls. For the 1,487 electric homes and anyone with a heat pump, it means coils, filters and refrigerant-side checks.
### Owners of rental buildings

Renters occupy 3,381 Milford households. A landlord who services the boiler before October is much less likely to get a cold-night call, and in a two-family house that call affects two households. Massachusetts expects rental heat to be maintained throughout the heating season, so a tune-up is cheaper than an emergency.
### A seasonal rhythm

- **Late summer to early fall:** heating tune-ups, before the first cold snaps.
- **Spring:** cooling checks on central air and mini-splits, before the first heat wave.
- **Any time:** a noise, a smell, short cycling or a rising fuel bill is a reason to call early.
### Signs your system is asking for help

- Short cycling, where the burner or compressor starts and stops every few minutes.
- Some rooms staying cold or hot while others are fine.
- A rising fuel or electric bill with no change in how you live.
- New noises, smells or soot around an oil burner.
### What to have ready when you call
The fuel you use, the approximate age of the system, the make and model on the nameplate if you can read it, and what you noticed. That lets us plan the visit properly.
Older systems benefit most. The median Milford home dates to 1970, and equipment in houses of that age is often in its second or third replacement cycle.

faq.q: How often should an oil boiler or furnace be serviced?
faq.a: Once a year is the usual rule for oil equipment, before the heating season. Skipping it lets soot build up, which can reduce efficiency and cause breakdowns in the coldest weeks.

faq.q: Should a landlord schedule a tune-up before winter?
faq.a: It is a good habit. A heating system that quits in a cold snap affects every tenant at once, and Massachusetts sets minimum indoor temperatures for rentals during the heating season.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Milford's homes span every era: 23.8% date from 1939 or earlier and 4.1% from 2010 or later. Leaky old houses and tight new ones have different air problems, and we start with the house.
body: ## Air quality in a town of mixed ages

The ACS 2022 splits Milford's 11,950 housing units into bands. 2,842 (23.8%) date from 1939 or earlier, 1,812 (15.2%) from 1940 to 1959, 3,583 (30.0%) from 1960 to 1979, 2,447 (20.5%) from 1980 to 1999, and 1,266 (10.6%) from 2000 on. Each band has a different air story.
### Older houses

Older homes tend to leak air through gaps, which dilutes some pollutants but also pulls in dust, pollen and damp basement air. Old ductwork can carry years of dust, and older materials can matter if you plan renovations, in which case a qualified specialist should test before work begins.
### Newer, tighter houses

A house built in the last decade or two, 491 Milford homes since 2010, is usually much tighter. That saves energy, and it also means moisture, cooking fumes and chemicals from furnishings stay inside unless ventilation does its job.
### Humidity through the seasons

Heating season dries indoor air, and cooling season brings humidity back. Both swings matter in an older house, where wood floors, plaster and basement walls respond to moisture. Keeping indoor humidity in a comfortable range protects the building as well as the people in it.
### What testing can and cannot tell you

Air quality testing can point to a problem such as high humidity, carbon monoxide or particles, but it is a snapshot. Fixing the source, whether a leaking duct, an unvented appliance or a wet basement, is what keeps the result from coming back.
### What we can do

- Upgrade filtration and keep filters changed on schedule.
- Control humidity with a dehumidifier or humidifier tied to the system.
- Add or fix ventilation so a tight house gets fresh air.
- Clean ducts that are visibly dirty or damaged, and fix the cause so they do not fill up again.

faq.q: Do I need my ducts cleaned?
faq.a: Not automatically. Cleaning makes sense when ducts are visibly dirty, have mold, or were damaged by pests or a renovation. We look at the system first and tell you whether cleaning would help.

faq.q: Why is my Milford basement damp?
faq.a: Basement moisture comes from the ground, from plumbing or from humid air meeting cool walls. A dehumidifier can control the air, but a leak or a grading problem has to be fixed at its source.
